summary: The machine has the runtime and credentials needed to start building the Node.js / Mongoose DocumentDB sample (Node 24, npx, npm via node, az signed-in, a reachable vector-capable DocumentDB cluster exposed via DOCUMENTDB_URI, and a specified sample database). Missing agent accelerators and CLI helpers (mongosh, documentdb MCP toolkit, DocumentDB Agent Kit, Azure/learn MCP entries) and several service facts that an agent would normally verify from docs are not available in the inventory; these are non-blocking for code work but will require caution and a few manual checks by the builder.
summary_points: Core build dependencies for the sample are present: node (v24), npx, git, and an authenticated az CLI; the skill.md confirms DOCUMENTDB_URI and database name sample_customer_360_01.

A live, vector-capable Azure DocumentDB cluster is available per skill.md (MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol, DiskANN/HNSW/IVF vector indexes) so the sample can be verified against it without provisioning resources.
Key developer accelerators (DocumentDB MCP Toolkit, DocumentDB Agent Kit, Azure and Learn MCP servers) are not installed and would speed tasks like schema inspection and authoritative doc fetches.

Several quiz items (connection string format, CLI/resource provider command group, AAD/Microsoft Entra auth for MongoDB wire protocol, exact index creation commands) could not be verified from the provided local artifacts and must be looked up by the builder.
Tools missing but recommended: mongosh (useful for hands-on verification). Its absence is not blocking: upserts and verification can be done programmatically from the sample code.
Verdict: ready_with_gaps — you can start the build, but add a few accelerators or perform a small number of doc checks before finalizing the sample and README.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: MongoDB connection strings follow mongodb:// or mongodb+srv://. For Azure DocumentDB (Cosmos DB MongoDB API) the host suffix is typically <account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com. Non-SRV form uses port 10255. Typical options required: ssl=true (or tls=true), replicaSet=globaldb, retryWrites=false. Example non-SRV: mongodb://<username>@<account>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/<dbname>?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false. Example SRV: mongodb+srv://<username>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/<dbname>?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false
confusions.grounded_answer: could not verify from available local artifacts.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixes formats used by many MongoDB-compatible services (Cosmos DB, MongoDB Atlas, Amazon DocumentDB) and can be mistaken without an authoritative doc to pin the exact host suffix and required options for this service.
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong connection string form or options may fail TLS negotiation or cause driver errors; the builder must not hard-code example connection strings and should rely on DOCUMENTDB_URI as instructed.
improvements: Add an explicit example connection string for this managed DocumentDB product to the skill.md or the agent-kit README (with placeholders and a reminder to use DOCUMENTDB_URI).

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Capacity is billed as Cosmos DB throughput: Request Units (RU/s) for provisioned throughput (can be fixed or autoscale). There is also a serverless mode for supported API/accounts. It is not billed by vCores for the MongoDB API (use RUs or serverless).
confusions.grounded_answer: could not verify from available local artifacts.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer reflects Cosmos DB RU model; the provided skill.md describes a compute tier (M30) in its run environment which suggests a vCore/compute-tier billing model in this product — the agent cannot reconcile without external docs.
confusions.build_risk: Mis-stating billing/throughput model in README or sample notes could lead users to wrong expectations; the builder should confirm billing model before documenting it.
improvements: Clarify billing model in the agent-kit README and sample README and include the official billing doc link via the Learn MCP server so agents can verify.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary supported auth for MongoDB API is account keys / username+password (username typically in the form <username>@<account> and password is the primary key). Resource tokens (for SDKs) exist for Cosmos DB SQL API, but MongoDB API commonly uses account keys. Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) data-plane authentication is not generally available for the MongoDB wire protocol (so drivers do not authenticate to the MongoDB API with AAD tokens in typical setups).
confusions.grounded_answer: could not verify from available local artifacts.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer follows common patterns for Cosmos DB's Mongo API and other managed Mongo services; without explicit docs the agent can't confirm whether this managed DocumentDB supports AAD data-plane auth.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes AAD data-plane auth is unavailable but it actually is supported, they may not use recommended secure auth flows; conversely, assuming AAD is supported when it is not would break authentication.
improvements: Add a short, authoritative section in skill.md or the agent-kit about supported authentication methods and an example of the recommended connection string pattern.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use standard MongoDB drivers (e.g., the Node.js mongodb driver or Mongoose). Do not use the Cosmos DB SQL-specific SDK if you intend to speak MongoDB protocol; there is no separate MongoDB-specific Azure SDK — the MongoDB driver is the correct client.
confusions.grounded_answer: Use Mongoose / standard MongoDB drivers for this sample; the sample prompt explicitly requests a Node.js Mongoose service.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: N/A — the sample itself specifies Mongoose.
confusions.build_risk: None for this sample; using Mongoose is the correct choice.

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically Cosmos DB / DocumentDB did not expose built-in vector index types via the MongoDB API. If vector search is required you normally integrate with Azure Cognitive Search or an external vector engine. Therefore there is no service-native MongoDB command to create DiskANN/HNSW/IVF indexes in the MongoDB API (no native db.collection.createIndex([...], {type:'hnsw' ...}) support).
confusions.grounded_answer: This environment is vector-capable and supports DiskANN, HNSW and IVF vector indexes (per the provided run environment description).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer reflects older Cosmos DB / Mongo API limitations; the provided skill.md explicitly states the cluster supports DiskANN/HNSW/IVF, showing this managed DocumentDB product exposes vector index capabilities.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumed vectors were unavailable they might omit vector index creation code or document an unnecessary external dependency; conversely, using an Atlas-style createIndex with a 'type' option might not be the exact command this service expects unless documented.
improvements: Document the exact index creation API and example commands for DiskANN/HNSW/IVF in the agent-kit and sample README so agents don't generalize from other MongoDB providers.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Full-text search is typically done by integrating Cosmos DB with Azure Cognitive Search (indexing Cosmos DB containers into an Azure Search index). Hybrid search (semantic + vector) is done in Azure Cognitive Search or an external search service; Cosmos DB's MongoDB API itself does not provide a first-class full-text + vector search engine.
confusions.grounded_answer: could not verify from available local artifacts.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer describes common Cosmos+Search patterns; skill.md mentions vector indexes on the cluster which suggests the product may have native vector capabilities that change the hybrid search story.
confusions.build_risk: If the sample documents only external search integration, readers may miss built-in vector capabilities available in this cluster.
improvements: Add a short canonical description in the agent-kit of how full-text and vector/hybrid search is supported for this service and provide example integrations.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos DB's MongoDB API implements a subset of the MongoDB wire protocol. Supported server versions historically lag upstream (common supported compatibility levels were 3.6, 4.0, 4.2, 4.4 and later additions), and not all MongoDB features are available. Commonly missing or limited features include some admin commands, server-side JavaScript, certain aggregation stages or collation behaviors, and some transactional or index features depending on the compatibility version. Expect to verify support for advanced features (change streams, transactions, some geo/aggregation operators) against the account's compatibility version.
confusions.grounded_answer: The provided run environment specifies MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol is supported on the reachable cluster; thus the cold answer is partly outdated/misplaced.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer is a generic description of Cosmos DB's past Mongo API compatibility limits; skill.md indicates this DocumentDB cluster speaks MongoDB 7.0, so the specific compatibility floor/ceiling in the cold answer is not authoritative for this product.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumed only older protocol versions were available they might avoid modern driver features or write compatibility shims unnecessarily, or conversely assume unsupported features during testing.
improvements: Explicitly state supported MongoDB wire protocol versions in the agent-kit and sample README; ensure the skill.md (or an MCP doc) is the canonical source for the cluster's reported wire protocol.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: There is an Azure Cosmos DB Emulator for the SQL API but it historically does not fully emulate the MongoDB wire protocol. For MongoDB API development you should run a local MongoDB server (official Docker image mongo) on the default port 27017, using the same MongoDB server version that your Cosmos account claims to support. There is no fully-featured local emulator that gives the exact Cosmos MongoDB behavior.
confusions.grounded_answer: could not verify from available local artifacts.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer reflects the common Cosmos emulator limitation; skill.md instructs to test against the live cluster rather than run a local gateway, so the local emulator story is unclear from local artifacts.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses a local plain Mongo image without acknowledging differences, tests may pass locally but fail against the managed cluster.
improvements: Add guidance in the sample README whether to run local Mongo for dev/testing and list any behavioral differences to watch for.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos DB exposes a Change Feed for the core (SQL) API; support for MongoDB change streams has been historically limited or unavailable. If you need change notifications on the MongoDB API, you typically must either use Cosmos DB Change Feed (via the SQL API) or poll/implement application-level hooks; there is no simple enablement flag for MongoDB change streams in older versions.
confusions.grounded_answer: could not verify from available local artifacts.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer is a safe generic statement; the cluster's MongoDB 7.0 support per skill.md suggests change stream support could differ, but no local doc clarifies whether Mongo change streams are supported.
confusions.build_risk: If the sample relied on change streams but the cluster doesn't support them, the sample would break; the sample avoids change-stream-based architecture by using upserts, so risk is limited.
improvements: Document change-stream support explicitly in the agent-kit and sample README, or include a short verification step the builder can run programmatically.

There isn't a separate special-purpose MCP agent required for Cosmos DB; the general Azure management plane and az CLI cover provisioning and management. For data-plane operations use the MongoDB drivers against the account endpoints.

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: The original preview service was called Azure DocumentDB; that product evolved into Azure Cosmos DB. "DocumentDB" historically refers to the SQL/JSON API implementation inside Cosmos DB. The Cosmos DB MongoDB API is a protocol compatibility layer (not the open-source MongoDB or Apache 'DocumentDB' project). The old name 'DocumentDB' is essentially superseded by Cosmos DB.
confusions.grounded_answer: partly correct but could not fully verify: the prompt and skill.md use the name 'Azure DocumentDB' for this managed MongoDB-compatible product and explicitly list it distinct from Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU) and from open-source DocumentDB. The local artifacts indicate the product is being referred to as 'Azure DocumentDB' in this environment.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer conflates historical names and Cosmos DB branding; the sample context intentionally distinguished Azure DocumentDB as a separate managed MongoDB-compatible product.
confusions.build_risk: Misnaming in the README or doc comments could confuse readers about which service the sample targets (Cosmos DB Mongo API vs managed DocumentDB cluster).
improvements: Add a brief historical note and a clear line in the sample README that this sample targets the managed 'Azure DocumentDB' MongoDB-compatible service (as provided in the run environment), distinct from legacy Cosmos DB naming.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Under the MongoDB API the underlying engine is Azure Cosmos DB's proprietary storage and execution engine with a MongoDB-compatible wire protocol layer. That means application code using standard MongoDB drivers will mostly work, but there are behavioral differences (query semantics, indexing, RU-based throttling, and some unsupported operators/commands). Test to confirm behavior for advanced features and tune RU usage.
confusions.grounded_answer: The sample run environment indicates a managed Azure DocumentDB cluster with a MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol and proprietary engine; application code should use standard MongoDB drivers/Mongoose but verify advanced features against the cluster.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: N/A — the skill.md affirms the managed product's MongoDB protocol compatibility and the need to verify advanced features.
confusions.build_risk: Low for the core sample; the builder must still test aggregation or index features if they rely on them.

confusions.question: What exact Mongoose connection invocation and options should the sample use to connect to the DocumentDB Mongo endpoint?
confusions.cold_answer: Example Node.js/Mongoose connect call: await mongoose.connect(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true, tls: true, tlsAllowInvalidCertificates: false, replicaSet: 'globaldb', retryWrites: false }); Replace placeholders in DOCUMENTDB_URI as necessary. Use TLS/SSL and disable retryWrites as recommended for Cosmos MongoDB API.

The agent cannot verify which options are required for this managed DocumentDB cluster without documentation for the targeted driver and the cluster's connection recommendations.
confusions.build_risk: Using deprecated or incorrect connection options may cause runtime warnings or connection failures; the builder must test the actual connect call against DOCUMENTDB_URI and prefer current Mongoose options for Node 24.

confusions.question: What index definition does this sample need for efficient upserts and lookups?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a unique index on the stable customer ID used for identity resolution. Example Mongo shell command: db.customers.createIndex({ customerId: 1 }, { unique: true, background: true });
confusions.grounded_answer: Create a unique index on customerId; the sample should create or ensure this index exists in sample_customer_360_01.customers for efficient upserts and deduplication.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: N/A — the sample prompt and cold answer are aligned on indexing needs.
confusions.build_risk: Not creating the index will make upserts slower and may allow duplicate stable customer IDs.

confusions.question: If change streams are not available, how will the sample perform idempotent upserts without losing other source sub-documents?
confusions.cold_answer: Use MongoDB upsert semantics with findOneAndUpdate and $set on nested sub-documents for each source. Example: db.customers.findOneAndUpdate({ customerId: id }, { $set: { 'sources.crm': crmAttrs, 'sources.ecom': ecomAttrs, updatedAt: new Date() } }, { upsert: true, returnDocument: 'after' }); This merges fields under sources.* and avoids overwriting unrelated source sub-documents.
confusions.grounded_answer: Use findOneAndUpdate / updateOne with { upsert: true } and $set on nested paths for each source to avoid overwriting other source sub-documents; this approach is consistent with the sample's prompt.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: N/A
confusions.build_risk: None if implemented as stated; ensure the update target uses nested field names and does not $set the root object.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the database sample_customer_360_01 and read the cluster connection string only from process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime; do not write the URI into any file or log.

Treat the cluster as speaking MongoDB 7.0 (test the Mongoose connect call against DOCUMENTDB_URI and prefer driver/Mongoose options compatible with Node.js 24 and MongoDB 7.0), and verify TLS is required at runtime rather than hard-coding driver option flags.
Create a unique index on the stable customerId (e.g., db.customers.createIndex({ customerId: 1 }, { unique: true })) during the sample seed/initialization to support efficient upserts.
Implement idempotent upserts using findOneAndUpdate/updateOne with { upsert: true } and $set on nested source sub-document paths (e.g., 'sources.crm'), to avoid overwriting unrelated fields.

If you plan to mention vectors or show vector-indexing, add an explicit, tested example of how to create DiskANN/HNSW/IVF indexes against the provided cluster (skill.md states they exist; the sample README must include the exact create-index call after testing it live).
